screens.title: Applying Routing Policies
screens.subtitle: How to make policies take effect: import, export, points of application, and verification.

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn not only how to write routing policies, but crucially where and when to attach them so they actually affect traffic. Policies control routes at their application points — most commonly as routes are received into the router with an import policy, or as routes are advertised outbound with an export policy. For BGP, that application happens at the group or neighbor level; for OSPF and RIP it is typically applied to redistribution or protocol-level export. You will also see how policies can be chained to create modular, maintainable checks, and why explicit accept and reject actions are safer than relying on implicit denial. Practical verification commands are part of the lesson: learning to compare what was received, what was installed, and what is being advertised is how you confirm policy behavior. By the end, you will understand when to use import versus export, how to structure chained policies, and which Junos commands help you validate and troubleshoot changes. Think about a recent routing change you made: could a misplaced import versus export have caused it? That question will help you apply what follows.

keyIdea.title: Primary idea
keyIdea.text: Routing policies must be applied at the correct protocol or interface point (import or export) to take effect; BGP uses neighbor/group application while OSPF/RIP typically use export for redistribution.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Applying Routing Policies
Applying Routing Policies
Understand import vs export, where to attach policies in Junos, and how to verify their effect across BGP, OSPF and static routes.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Orientation

Policies must be applied where routing information enters or leaves: import controls received routes; export controls advertised routes. Knowing the application point prevents common mistakes.

Why it matters

Incorrect application can silently block routes or advertise unwanted prefixes. Verification commands let you confirm whether changes took effect as intended.

Concept connections
Import
Filters or modifies routes received from a neighbor before installation.
Export
Controls which local routes are advertised to peers or redistributed into other protocols.
Chaining
Sequence multiple policies so each handles a focused task, using next-policy to continue evaluation.
Explore Key Topics
BGP application
Apply import/export per neighbor or group to control inbound/outbound prefixes.
OSPF / RIP export
Use export policies to control redistribution from direct, static, or BGP into OSPF or RIP.
Verify & troubleshoot
Use show route receive-protocol and show route advertising-protocol to compare before and after policy effects.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Four competencies you will build and verify during this chapter.

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to apply, verify, and troubleshoot routing policies across common protocols. First, you will learn to apply policies for both import and export operations — this includes understanding the practical difference between filtering routes received from peers and filtering routes you advertise. Second, you'll practice applying policies at interface-specific or static-route points when you want to control direct or redistributed routes. Third, you'll learn to design chained policies so each module performs a focused function and the sequence achieves complex goals. Finally, you will master Junos verification commands and troubleshooting steps to confirm policy behavior. Each objective focuses on measurable tasks: configuring import/export on a BGP neighbor, creating export rules for OSPF redistribution, constructing policy chains that use next-policy, and using show route commands to compare pre- and post-policy route sets. These skills matter because incorrect application or missing verification is a common cause of network outages. You will also see example commands and a hands-on walkthrough so you can practice safely in a lab environment.

keyIdea.title: Competency focus
keyIdea.text: Apply import/export correctly, handle interface/static applications, chain policies modularly, and verify with Junos show commands.

content.html:

screens.title: Skills and verification steps
screens.subtitle: What you should be able to do and how to prove it in Junos.

narration.text: This second objectives slide expands the same four competencies with concrete verification steps and a mnemonic to help you remember. For import and export application, practice by applying a policy to a BGP neighbor and using show route receive-protocol and show route protocol to observe the difference. For interface or static applications, test by creating a static route, applying an import filter under routing-options static if available, and confirming whether the route is active. For policy chaining, create focused policy statements — for example one policy to reject bogons and another to set local preference — then chain them so evaluation continues using next-policy. Finally, verification: run show policy-options to inspect statements, then compare show route advertising-protocol and show route receive-protocol for a neighbor to see pre- and post-policy state. A helpful mnemonic is I-C-V-T: Identify application point, Create focused terms, Verify effects, Test in lab. These steps make policy rollouts safer and faster to troubleshoot when something does not behave as expected.

keyIdea.title: How to prove competency
keyIdea.text: Confirm each objective with show-policy, show-route receive/advertising-protocol comparisons, and lab testing before production commits.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Objectives — Details
Objective 1: Import / Export

Practice applying a policy to a BGP neighbor and use show route receive-protocol to see what arrived and show route protocol bgp to see what was installed after import filtering.

Objective 2: Interface/Static

Apply filters for static or direct routes when multiple candidates exist and verify the active route in the routing table after commit.

Objective 3: Policy chaining

Design small policies and chain them using next-policy to continue evaluation only when intended; test chain order in a lab.

Objective 4: Verify & Troubleshoot

Use show policy-options and the advertising/receive protocol commands to compare expected vs actual behavior and run commit check before committing.

screens.title: Import and Export: Definition and effect
screens.subtitle: What import and export actually do to routing information.

narration.text: An import policy evaluates routes as they are received from a neighbor or as they are considered for installation into the local routing table. When a route arrives from a peer, an import policy can filter it out, modify attributes, or accept it for installation. This is essential for inbound traffic engineering, preventing unwanted prefixes, and ensuring only acceptable routes reach the local RIB. An export policy evaluates routes before the router advertises them to a neighbor or before redistributing into another protocol. It is the control point for what you allow the network to learn from you. A concrete example: if a router receives a full routing table from a peer but you only want a few prefixes, an import policy that rejects everything except those few will prevent pollution of your routing table. A common misconception is to think import and export are interchangeable; they operate at opposite times. Import affects what you install, export affects what others learn from you. A takeaway question: if a prefix is absent both from your routing table and your neighbor's received list, did you apply the wrong direction of policy? That diagnostic will help you quickly isolate direction-related issues.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Import filters incoming routes before installation; export filters outgoing advertisements before they are sent.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Import & Export
Definition and behaviour
Import and export are evaluation points in the route-processing pipeline. Import acts on received routes before they are installed; export acts on local routes before advertisement.
Import — key points
  • Filters or modifies received routes before installation.
  • Used for inbound traffic engineering and security.
Export — key points
  • Controls what local routes are advertised or redistributed.
  • Critical for controlling outbound advertisements and redistribution sets.
Key Takeaway

Import changes what you accept; export changes what others see. Direction matters for troubleshooting.

Concrete example
set protocols bgp group EXTERNAL_PEER neighbor 203.0.113.2 import INBOUND_FILTER
set protocols bgp group EXTERNAL_PEER neighbor 203.0.113.2 export OUTBOUND_ADVERTISE
In this configuration the import policy is applied to routes received from 203.0.113.2, while the export policy filters what is sent to that neighbor.
Common misconception
Confusing import and export is common. If your router is not installing expected prefixes, first check receive-protocol output to confirm what arrived before blaming export filters.

screens.title: Applying policies in BGP
screens.subtitle: Group-level and neighbor-level application, with override behavior.

narration.text: BGP applies routing policies at the group or neighbor level in Junos. When you attach an import or export policy to a group, it affects all neighbors that belong to that group. If you attach a policy directly to a neighbor, it overrides the group-level policy for that neighbor. This design lets you create a common default at group level and specialize per neighbor when needed. A concrete example: set an import policy on the group that performs general filtering, then for a specific neighbor add a neighbor-level import to tighten restrictions for that peer. Remember the evaluation: import policies act on routes received from the peer before installation; export policies act on routes you will advertise. A common mistake is assuming a policy applied to the group will not be overridden; neighbor-level configuration takes precedence. When building policies for BGP groups, maintain clear names and document exceptions so overrides are visible during review. For practical verification, use show protocols bgp group detail or show protocols bgp neighbor detail to confirm which policies are active, and compare receive and installed route sets with show route receive-protocol and show route protocol bgp. How might you structure default filtering and per-peer exceptions for a mixed transit and customer environment?

keyIdea.title: BGP specifics
keyIdea.text: Policies can be applied at group or neighbor levels; neighbor-level policies override group-level settings, enabling defaults and exceptions.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › BGP Application
Process: Group vs Neighbor
Apply shared behavior at the group level and use neighbor-level policies for exceptions. The neighbor-level setting takes precedence over the group setting.
Group-level
Ideal for default filters and common transformations for multiple peers.
Neighbor-level
Use for per-peer exceptions and tighter controls; this overrides the group policy.
Verification commands
show protocols bgp group <group-name> detail • show protocols bgp neighbor <address> detail
Example scenario
set protocols bgp group EXTERNAL_PEER type external
set protocols bgp group EXTERNAL_PEER import GROUP_IN
set protocols bgp group EXTERNAL_PEER neighbor 203.0.113.2 import PEER_SPECIFIC_IN
In this setup GROUP_IN applies to all group peers, but PEER_SPECIFIC_IN overrides for 203.0.113.2 so that peer receives a tighter inbound filter.
Common mistake
Expecting group policies to always take effect. If a neighbor has its own policy, it will replace the group's policy for that neighbor.

screens.title: Applying policies in OSPF and RIP
screens.subtitle: How export policies control redistribution and what to match.

narration.text: In OSPF and RIP, policies are most often used to control redistribution — the process of advertising routes learned by other protocols, direct interfaces, or static configuration into the IGP. An export policy attached to the OSPF or RIP process selects which routes are allowed into the protocol. For example, an OSPF export policy can match protocol direct, protocol static, or protocol bgp and then accept selected routes for redistribution. Without an explicit export policy, redistribution typically will not happen or may behave in ways you do not intend. A concrete command from Junos is set protocols ospf export OSPF_REDISTRIBUTION_POLICY. This policy would usually contain terms that match the source protocol and specific prefixes, then accept those chosen routes. A common misconception is to expect OSPF to automatically leak routes between areas or from other protocols; redistribution must be explicit and carefully controlled. The key takeaway is to treat export policies for IGPs as a gate: only allow the intended routes to cross into the IGP, and test the resulting LSDB or routing table to confirm the redistributed prefixes appear where expected.

keyIdea.title: OSPF/RIP export
keyIdea.text: Export policies control which non-IGP routes are redistributed into OSPF or RIP by matching source protocols and prefixes.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › OSPF & RIP Export
Definition: Redistribution gate
Use export policies to control which direct, static, or BGP routes are redistributed into OSPF or RIP. This prevents uncontrolled flooding of prefixes into the IGP.
Match examples
  • protocol direct
  • protocol static
  • protocol bgp
Key Takeaway

Export to IGPs controls redistribution; always match protocol and prefix to avoid unintended advertisements.

Code example
# Example for OSPF export policy
set protocols ospf export OSPF_REDISTRIBUTION_POLICY

# Policy would match protocol direct, static, or bgp and accept selected routes
Attach this policy to the OSPF process so only the intended routes become LSAs in OSPF or are advertised by RIP.
Common misconception
Believing IGPs automatically share routes between areas or protocols. Redistribution requires explicit export configuration and careful matching.

screens.title: Applying policies to static and direct routes
screens.subtitle: When and how to filter static or directly connected routes.

narration.text: Policies can also be applied to control which static or direct routes are installed into the routing table. Though less common than protocol-level application, this is useful when multiple static routes or conditional static configuration exists and you want to choose which one is active. For example, you might use an import policy under routing-options static to filter which static routes are considered active. The practical effect is that static configuration alone does not guarantee installation if an import filter blocks it. This is particularly relevant in complex failure scenarios where multiple static candidates exist; a policy lets you prefer one and reject others without changing the underlying static statements. A common misconception is to assume static routes are always active if configured; policy checks can prevent installation. When using static import filters, always run commit check first and then verify the active route with show route protocol static to confirm which static entry is present. Consider whether a dynamic protocol will also influence selection; static filters affect installation but route selection still follows RIB logic when multiple candidates exist.

keyIdea.title: Static route control
keyIdea.text: You can filter static and direct routes during installation by applying import policies under routing-options, allowing fine-grained control over which static routes become active.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Static & Direct Routes
When to apply static route policies
Use import policies under routing-options static to pick which configured static routes are installed, especially when multiple candidates exist for the same prefix.
Practical uses
  • Choose a preferred static route among alternatives
  • Prevent accidental static advertisement via redistribution
Verification
Use show route protocol static to confirm installation. Run commit check before committing policy changes to avoid syntax issues.
Analogy
Think of policies as a gatekeeper: static routes exist in config drawers, but the gate decides which ones are allowed onto the stage of the routing table.
Key takeaway
Applying import policies to static routes gives operational control without changing static configuration, simplifying swaps and tests.

screens.title: Designing and using policy chaining
screens.subtitle: How policies sequence with next-policy and why modular design helps.

narration.text: Policy chaining is the technique of applying multiple policies in a defined sequence so that each policy can handle a focused task. When Junos evaluates import [ POLICY_A POLICY_B POLICY_C ] it processes POLICY_A first. If POLICY_A explicitly accepts or rejects a route, evaluation stops. If POLICY_A uses then next-policy, the route is passed to POLICY_B for further evaluation. This allows modular design: one policy can reject bogon prefixes, another can set attributes such as local preference, and a final policy can perform prefix accepts or rejects. The practical benefit is easier testing and clearer change control — small policies are easier to audit and reason about than one monolithic statement. A common error is forgetting to include next-policy when you expect subsequent checks to run; the default accept or reject will stop processing. Always document the intended flow and test each module in isolation before chaining. A concrete design pattern is 'filter then tag then accept': first remove undesired prefixes, then set attributes on those you will allow, then finalize with an accept term. This pattern reduces mistakes and simplifies rollback.

keyIdea.title: Chaining mechanics
keyIdea.text: Use next-policy to pass evaluation to the next policy; explicit accept/reject stops evaluation early. Keep policies small and focused.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Policy Chaining
How chaining works
List policies in the desired order. Each policy can accept, reject, or pass the route to the next policy using next-policy. This lets you build modular, testable rule sets.
Pattern: Filter → Tag → Accept
First policy removes bad prefixes, second sets attributes, third finalizes acceptance.
Gotcha
Missing next-policy will stop evaluation; explicit actions are safer than implicit denies.
Key Takeaway

Design small policies and chain them deliberately. Use next-policy only when you want evaluation to continue.

Example callout
Imagine POLICY_A rejects bogons with then reject, POLICY_B sets local preference for customer routes with then next-policy, and POLICY_C accepts remaining customer prefixes. Evaluation follows the listed sequence and stops when a policy issues accept or reject.
Check your understanding
If a route should be accepted by POLICY_C but POLICY_B lacks next-policy, what happens? You will discover the route is either accepted or rejected earlier, so include next-policy when you intend continuation.

screens.title: Policy design best practices
screens.subtitle: Specificity, explicit actions, modularity, naming, documentation, and testing.

narration.text: Good policy design reduces mistakes and simplifies troubleshooting. Start with specificity: place the more specific terms at the top of a policy so they match before broader rules. Always use explicit then accept or then reject actions; relying on implicit deny makes it harder to understand why a route was dropped. Modular design — breaking a large requirement into smaller policies — supports chaining and clearer audits. Use clear, descriptive names for policy-statements, terms, prefix-lists and communities so a reviewer immediately understands intent. Document each policy's purpose in configuration comments or external documentation so the operational owner can trace why the policy exists. Finally, test in a lab environment before committing to production; incorrect policies can cause wide routing outages. A concrete approach is to write a bogon-rejection policy, an attribute-setting policy, and a final accept/reject policy, then chain them. Running commit check will catch syntax errors; after commit, verify with show policy-options and show route commands to confirm behavior. The core insight is that thoughtful structure and testing are as important as the rules themselves when policy mistakes can affect many networks.

keyIdea.title: Design checklist
keyIdea.text: Be specific, use explicit actions, keep policies modular, name clearly, document purpose, and always test in lab before production.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Best Practices
Checklist for policy design
  • Specificity: Put specific terms first.
  • Explicit actions: Use then accept/then reject.
  • Modular design: One task per policy, chain them.
  • Clear naming: Descriptive names for fast review.
  • Documentation: Explain purpose and intent.
  • Testing: Lab test and commit check before production.
Example structure
Split rules into three policies: reject bogons, set attributes for customers, final accept/reject list. Chain them so the route flows through each focused check.
Common mistake
Creating one large policy that is hard to test and debug. Break problems into smaller policies and chain them instead.

screens.title: Commands to verify policy application
screens.subtitle: What to run to inspect policies, received routes, and advertised routes.

narration.text: Verification is where policy work becomes trustworthy. Several Junos commands are essential: show policy-options displays the entire policy configuration, including prefix-lists and communities — use it to confirm match conditions and actions. To inspect what you received from a BGP neighbor before import filtering, use show route receive-protocol bgp neighbor-address; this reveals the incoming prefixes as announced. To see what routes are installed under BGP after import evaluation, use show route protocol bgp detail for attributes like local preference or community modifications. To check outbound advertisements after export policy processing, run show route advertising-protocol bgp neighbor-address to see the set of prefixes being sent. commit check helps catch configuration syntax issues before commit. A troubleshooting workflow is to compare show route receive-protocol output with show route advertising-protocol output and the installed route set. If differences exist, the policy that transforms or rejects routes is likely the cause. A common misconception is to rely on only one command; combine these outputs to find where a route disappeared or was modified. Always document the verification steps you used for reproducibility. Commands to verify policy application means use show policy-options, show route receive-protocol, show route protocol bgp detail, and show route advertising-protocol to compare before and after policy effects.. In practical terms, what to run to inspect policies, received routes, and advertised routes.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Verify commands
keyIdea.text: Use show policy-options, show route receive-protocol, show route protocol bgp detail, and show route advertising-protocol to compare before and after policy effects.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Verification Commands
Common verification commands
  • show policy-options — inspect policy statements and prefix-lists
  • show route receive-protocol bgp <neighbor-address> — routes received before import
  • show route protocol bgp <prefix> detail — installed BGP route attributes
  • show route advertising-protocol bgp <neighbor-address> — routes advertised after export
  • commit check — validate configuration syntax before commit
Walkthrough example
# Inspect policy config
show policy-options

# Compare received vs advertised routes
show route receive-protocol bgp 203.0.113.2
show route advertising-protocol bgp 203.0.113.2

# Check installed attributes
show route protocol bgp 192.0.2.0/24 detail
Compare the three outputs to locate whether a route was blocked on import, modified by a policy, or filtered on export.

screens.title: Clearing BGP sessions and soft-in/soft-out
screens.subtitle: When to use soft resets and when to clear the session entirely.

narration.text: After changing policies, especially import or export rules, you may need to re-evaluate what the peer sends or what you advertise. Junos offers two helpful approaches: soft reset and full clear. A soft-in reprocesses received routes against the current import policy without tearing down the TCP session; this is often enough when you've changed import filters and want to re-evaluate inbound routes. A soft-out forces re-advertisement so the neighbor receives updates based on the latest export policy without resetting the session. A full clear re-establishes the session completely and is useful when the session state is suspect or when both sides need a clean handshake. Use soft-in and soft-out to minimize traffic disruption; they are the usual first step after policy tweaks. Remember to verify after the reset using show route receive-protocol and show route advertising-protocol to confirm the intended effect. A common mistake is to skip the soft reset and assume policies will apply without re-evaluation; routes learned earlier may remain until reprocessed. Always plan clears during maintenance windows and document the expected outcome. Clearing BGP sessions and soft-in/soft-out means use soft-in to re-evaluate inbound routes against import policies and soft-out to re-advertise with updated export policies. full clear rebuilds the session if needed.. In practical terms, when to use soft resets and when to clear the session entirely.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Session refresh
keyIdea.text: Use soft-in to re-evaluate inbound routes against import policies and soft-out to re-advertise with updated export policies. Full clear rebuilds the session if needed.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › BGP Session Management
Soft-in and soft-out explained
Use soft-in to reprocess received routes against new import policies without tearing down the session. Use soft-out to re-advertise routes after export policy changes. Full clears rebuild the session when required.
When to use
Try soft-in/soft-out after policy changes to minimize disruption; use full clear only if session state is inconsistent or troubleshooting requires a clean handshake.
Key Takeaway

Prefer soft resets for policy re-evaluation; they minimize impact while applying policy changes.

Operational checklist
  • Change policy in configuration and commit.
  • Run commit check first to catch syntax issues.
  • Run clear bgp neighbor <addr> soft-in or soft-out as needed.
  • Verify with show route receive-protocol and show route advertising-protocol.
Common mistake
Not re-evaluating sessions after policy changes and assuming the new policy immediately applied to in-memory routes.

screens.title: Apply an export policy to advertise a loopback
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step lab walkthrough using the example configuration.

narration.text: Let's walk through the hands-on activity provided in the chapter: configuring an export policy that advertises only a specific loopback address to a BGP neighbor. Start by ensuring the loopback exists. Then create a prefix-list that contains the loopback prefix you want to advertise. Next, build an export policy with a term that matches direct protocol and the prefix-list, accepting that term, and a final term that rejects everything else. Apply the export policy to the BGP group or neighbor. Commit the configuration and run show policy-options policy-statement to confirm the policy content. If a BGP session exists, run show route advertising-protocol bgp <neighbor-ip> to confirm only the desired loopback is being advertised. If the route does not appear, consider soft-out to re-advertise after policy changes. This sequence teaches the core lifecycle: create route, match it with a prefix-list, create a policy that accepts it and rejects others, attach the policy, and verify. A useful lab practice is to test the policy in a non-production sandbox and validate with the show commands before applying changes on live routers. Apply an export policy to advertise a loopback means create loopback, build prefix-list, write export policy to accept the loopback and reject others, apply to bgp, commit, and verify advertising-protocol output.. In practical terms, step-by-step lab walkthrough using the example configuration.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lab flow
keyIdea.text: Create loopback, build prefix-list, write export policy to accept the loopback and reject others, apply to BGP, commit, and verify advertising-protocol output.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Hands-on Activity
Step-by-step commands
set interfaces lo0 unit 0 family inet address 192.168.1.1/32

set policy-options prefix-list ADVERTISED_LOOPS {
  192.168.1.1/32;
}

set policy-options policy-statement EXPORT_DIRECT_ROUTES term ALLOW_LO0 from protocol direct
set policy-options policy-statement EXPORT_DIRECT_ROUTES term ALLOW_LO0 from prefix-list ADVERTISED_LOOPS
set policy-options policy-statement EXPORT_DIRECT_ROUTES term ALLOW_LO0 then accept

set policy-options policy-statement EXPORT_DIRECT_ROUTES term REJECT_ALL_OTHERS then reject

set protocols bgp group MY_EXTERNAL_PEER type external
set protocols bgp group MY_EXTERNAL_PEER neighbor 10.0.0.2
set protocols bgp group MY_EXTERNAL_PEER export EXPORT_DIRECT_ROUTES

commit and-quit
show policy-options policy-statement EXPORT_DIRECT_ROUTES
show protocols bgp group MY_EXTERNAL_PEER
show route advertising-protocol bgp 10.0.0.2
Notes and verification
After commit, the advertising-protocol output should list only 192.168.1.1/32 if the export policy works. If not present, try soft-out to re-advertise or check the prefix-list and term matches. Use show policy-options to inspect any mismatches or typos.
Key takeaway
This lab ties together loopback config, prefix-lists, export policy creation, application to BGP, and verification — the full policy lifecycle in practice.

screens.title: Troubleshooting common policy errors
screens.subtitle: Import vs export confusion, chaining mistakes, implicit deny, and missing session refresh.

narration.text: Common mistakes during policy deployment are predictable and avoidable if you check the right places. The first is applying import when you intended export or vice versa; remember import affects incoming routes and export controls outgoing advertisements. Second, chaining errors — forgetting next-policy or next-term — leave evaluation prematurely stopped. Third, relying on implicit deny without explicit accept rules makes it harder to explain why a route is missing. Fourth, failing to refresh BGP sessions after applying policies may leave previous route sets in place, so use soft-in or soft-out as appropriate. Finally, misnaming prefix-lists or policy terms or making typographical errors often show up as unexpected behavior; show policy-options helps reveal these mistakes. A troubleshooting workflow begins with show policy-options to validate configuration, then compares show route receive-protocol, show route protocol bgp detail, and show route advertising-protocol to find where a route changed or disappeared. If the route is in receive-protocol but not installed, import is blocking it; if installed but not advertised, export is blocking it. This logical narrowing quickly isolates the issue so you can correct the policy.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshooting flow
keyIdea.text: Compare receive-protocol, installed routes, and advertising-protocol to locate where a route was blocked or modified; refresh sessions when necessary.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Common Mistakes
Frequent errors
  • Using import where export was intended or the reverse.
  • Incorrect chaining: missing next-policy causes unexpected stops.
  • Relying on implicit deny rather than explicit accept/reject.
  • Not running soft-in/soft-out after policy changes.
  • Typographical mistakes in policy or prefix-list names.
Troubleshooting checklist
1. show policy-options to check configuration.
2. show route receive-protocol bgp <neighbor> to see what arrived.
3. show route protocol bgp <prefix> detail to inspect attributes after import.
4. show route advertising-protocol bgp <neighbor> to view outbound advertising.
5. soft-in/soft-out or clear the session if routes are not re-evaluated.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Three core concepts to keep in mind when applying routing policies.

narration.text: Here are three compact reminders to carry forward. Import policy: this is applied to routes received before they are installed and is your control point for inbound filtering and attribute modification. Export policy: this controls what your router advertises or redistributes into other protocols and is essential for outbound traffic engineering and controlled redistribution. Policy chaining: Junos lets you list policies in sequence and continue evaluation with next-policy, which enables modular policy design — small focused policies are easier to test and maintain. Keep these three concepts straight as you design configuration and verification workflows. When you're unsure where a route disappeared, compare receive-protocol, installed routes, and advertising-protocol outputs to find which control point affected the route.
